summary:
**Orbit Check** is an offline health monitoring tool that helps astronauts track and act on their own health on long-duration missions. Each day, a crew member logs resting heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, weight, sleep, mood, stress, exercise, radiation dose, cabin CO₂ and symptoms. The software compares these readings with the astronaut’s personal baseline and adjustable thresholds. It rates five domains (cardiovascular and fluid shift, bone and muscle, immune and skin, behavior and sleep, radiation and air) as nominal, watch or act now, and combines them into a Crew Health Index. Trend analysis warns days before a metric crosses an alert limit, and every flag comes with concrete actions. A crew view highlights shared problems such as degrading cabin air, and a structured report can go to ground when a link is available.

This addresses the challenge directly. It covers radiation, isolation, altered gravity and closed-environment hazards, and puts monitoring in the astronaut’s hands. On Moon or Mars missions, communication delays make real-time ground support impractical, so crews must detect and respond to health changes early and autonomously. Thresholds are illustrative and need clinical validation.
details:
What it does and how it works

Orbit Check is a web app that lets an astronaut monitor their own health on a long mission. Each day the crew member logs resting heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, weight, sleep, mood, stress, exercise, radiation dose, cabin CO₂ and eight symptoms. The app compares each reading with the person’s own baseline (their first five check-ins) and with editable alert thresholds. It rates five domains as nominal, watch or act now: cardio and fluid shift, bone and muscle, immune and skin, behavior and sleep, radiation and air. Each flag shows the reason behind it and a concrete next step. The domain ratings combine into a 0–100 Crew Health Index, which loses 12 points per domain on watch and 30 per domain on act now. A trend fit over the last ten check-ins warns when a metric is on course to cross its threshold within two weeks. A crew roster shows every member’s index. If two or more members have radiation or cabin-air flags, the app prompts the crew to check shared systems first. It also writes a structured SBAR report (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) to send to the ground when the link allows.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It works fully offline and stores data only on the device, so it keeps working during communication delays or loss of signal.
  • Every flag is explained, so the astronaut can see why it fired.
  • Trend warnings give time to act before a problem becomes an emergency.
  • Shared-environment alerts separate a crew-wide cause from an individual one.

The intended impact is earlier, better-informed self-care and faster escalation, which matters on Moon and Mars missions where ground support is delayed. It is also aimed at reducing the risks the challenge names: immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events and behavioral health problems.

Tools and technology

  • App: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with inline SVG charts and browser local storage. There are no frameworks or external libraries. It runs on any device with a browser, and no special hardware is needed.
  • Development: written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), then published as a Claude artifact. The slide deck was built with the Slides artifact type.
  • Video: Node.js with jsdom ran the real app to extract its output. Python with Pillow drew the frames, and ffmpeg encoded the video.

What is creative about it

It treats the astronaut as the first responder, and it personalizes every judgment to the individual’s baseline instead of population norms. It predicts problems from trends rather than only reacting to thresholds, and it reasons across the whole crew to spot environmental causes. The report is designed for store-and-forward communication over a delayed link.

Factors considered

  • Autonomy under communication delay, and offline operation.
  • Privacy: nothing leaves the device.
  • Explainability, so the astronaut can trust and check each flag.
  • Short daily effort, about a minute.
  • Safety: a “hopeless or unsafe” symptom escalates immediately to a psychologist call.
  • Honesty about limits.

Limits

The thresholds and radiation rates (about 0.5 mSv/day in low Earth orbit and 1.8 in deep space) are illustrative and not clinically validated. Inputs are self-reported, with no wearable or sensor integration yet. The demo data is simulated. This is decision support, not a diagnosis. I tested the app by running it in a headless simulator, not on real devices or with clinicians. A lot of the UI work is AI-generated, and every artifact discloses that.

Natural next steps are clinical review of the thresholds, wearable and dosimeter feeds, and encrypted crew-shared storage.
